title: POS-integrated vs standalone phone AI for restaurants
seoTitle: POS-integrated vs standalone phone AI | ROAL
description: Compare POS-integrated and standalone phone AI for restaurants, including setup, cost, order flow, and which option fits best.
question: Should I use POS-integrated or standalone phone AI for restaurant phone orders?
answer: For most independent restaurants, the choice comes down to where the order ticket needs to land and how much setup you want. A POS-integrated phone AI can move orders into your existing system, while a standalone phone AI usually sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen and works faster to launch. If your POS is already the center of your workflow, integration may matter; if you want quick phone ordering without a heavy setup, standalone is often the simpler path.
summary: You’ll learn which phone AI setup fits your restaurant workflow, budget, and busy shifts.
intro:
POS-integrated and standalone phone AI both answer the phone and take orders, but they fit different restaurant setups. The right choice depends on how your kitchen runs, how much you want to change, and whether you need the order to land inside your POS or just get to the kitchen fast.

If you are comparing [comparisons](/compare) because calls are slipping through during rushes, think in practical terms: What happens after the caller says “pickup for 7:15”? Do you need the order in your POS, or do you mainly need a clean ticket that your team can start right away?

sections.h2: What is the real difference between POS-integrated and standalone phone AI?
sections.body:
The simplest way to think about it is this: POS-integrated phone AI tries to place the order into your existing order system, while standalone phone AI focuses on taking the order correctly and sending it to your kitchen workflow.

For a pizza shop, that might mean the caller says, “One large pepperoni, extra cheese, thin crust, no onions.” A POS-integrated setup aims to pass that into the POS. A standalone setup sends a ticket to the kitchen screen so staff can fire it from there. Both can be useful. The difference is where your team wants to work.

Here is a quick owner checklist:
- Do you already run everything through your POS?
- Do kitchen staff rely on a separate screen for tickets?
- Do you need the phone host to live inside one system, or just hand off the order cleanly?
- Do you want the fastest setup, or do you want tighter system matching?

ROAL is on the standalone side: it answers the call, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That can be enough for many small restaurants that just want the phone covered and the tickets organized.

sections.h2: How does the order flow change for your staff?
sections.body:
The order flow matters more than the label. In a busy deli or takeout spot, every extra handoff can slow service. A good setup should make the caller feel heard and make the kitchen see the ticket clearly.

Use this simple flow to compare the two:

| Step | POS-integrated phone AI | Standalone phone AI |
|---|---|---|
| Caller orders | Host collects items, sizes, modifiers, notes | Host collects items, sizes, modifiers, notes |
| Order handoff | Order is sent into your POS workflow | Order is sent to the kitchen screen |
| Staff review | Cashier or manager checks POS | Kitchen or counter staff checks ticket |
| Payment | Usually handled by your existing process | Payment is still handled by your existing process |

A practical example: say your average pickup order is $28. If the host captures three extra orders on a busy Friday, that is $84 in sales you can compare against your own margins. Plug in your own average ticket and your own call volume.

A good phone host should also do the little things: quote a ready time, confirm the order back, collect the caller’s name and phone, and skip sold-out items. That reduces back-and-forth for staff, whether the system is integrated or standalone.

sections.h2: What does setup look like when you are already busy?
sections.body:
Setup is where many owners feel the difference most. POS-integrated setups can take more planning because someone has to line up menus, modifiers, item names, and the way orders should land in your existing system. Standalone phone AI is often easier when you want something live quickly and do not want to rework your whole workflow.

With ROAL, the setup is straightforward: paste your website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and it reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages. You can also upload a menu in any format. The owner can test-call it in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed. That is useful if you want to hear how it handles your own menu items before forwarding calls.

Use this setup checklist:
1. Check that your menu and prices are current.
2. Decide which calls should go to the host: all calls, busy calls, or unanswered calls.
3. Test a few real menu items and modifiers.
4. Make sure sold-out items are marked so they are not offered.
5. Confirm who reviews questions the host could not answer.

If you want a simple way to start comparing options, [build a free test host](/try) and see how your actual menu sounds on the phone.

sections.h2: How much should you budget for each option?
sections.body:
Budget is not just about sticker price. It is also about how the pricing matches your call volume and your order volume.

Many AI phone tools for restaurants charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often roughly $79 to $599 whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can add up fast on larger tickets.

ROAL uses a different model: $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free, and billing happens monthly.

Here is a simple owner calculation you can copy:
- Say you complete 200 phone orders in a month.
- At $0.90 each, that would be $180.
- If your average order is $28, that is $5,600 in phone order sales.

Now plug in your own numbers. If you only get a smaller number of phone orders, a pay-per-order model may fit better than a fixed monthly plan. If you get very high phone volume, compare the total monthly cost against your current labor and missed-call risk. [Pricing](/pricing) shows the current ROAL model clearly.

sections.h2: When does a standalone phone host make more sense?
sections.body:
Standalone usually makes more sense when your restaurant wants speed, simplicity, or a cleaner handoff than your current phone process. It can be the better fit for pizza shops, delis, family restaurants, and takeout spots that already have a kitchen screen and do not want to rebuild their whole stack.

A standalone setup often fits if:
- Your team already works from kitchen tickets.
- Your POS is mostly for checkout, not for phone order entry.
- You want to launch quickly with less technical setup.
- You care more about answering the phone and getting the order to the kitchen than about changing your whole ordering system.

A POS-integrated setup can be worth it if your staff truly needs every order to appear inside the same place they already use for in-store and online work. That can reduce duplication, but it can also mean more setup and more points to check.

ROAL also handles practical side tasks that matter during rushes: it can answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions; speak the caller’s language; take reservation requests; and hand allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That is often enough for a busy independent shop that wants the phone covered without changing its day-to-day routine.

sections.h2: What should you test before you choose one?
sections.body:
Do a real-world test, not a feature checklist alone. The best phone AI for your place is the one that matches your menu, your staff habits, and your busiest calls.

Test these five things:
1. A basic pickup order with one modifier.
2. A larger order with several items and notes.
3. A caller asking about hours, address, and parking.
4. A sold-out item that should not be offered.
5. A complaint or allergy-sensitive question that should reach staff.

Example script to use on the call: “I need two chicken sandwiches, one no mayo, and a side of fries. Can I pick up in 25 minutes?” If the host handles that clearly, confirms the name and phone, and gives a ready time that makes sense, you are off to a good start.

Ask your team one more question: “Where do we want the ticket to land?” If the answer is the kitchen screen, standalone may be enough. If the answer is your POS, then POS integration may be more important. If you run multiple locations, check whether each location needs its own phone line and menu setup. ROAL supports multi-location menus in the dashboard, which helps when one owner manages several spots.

takeaways: POS-integrated phone AI fits restaurants that need orders inside their existing system.
Standalone phone AI is often simpler when your team mainly needs clean kitchen tickets.
Compare pricing by your actual order volume, not just the monthly sticker price.
Test real menu items, modifiers, sold-out items, and staff handoff before you decide.
